**The new task is not fully determined: two readings fit all the examples equally well and predict opposite colours.**

**Y components (which bit each one reads)**
- **Y4 = bit 2.** In X6-Y4-Z3, every red input has 0 in bit 2 of both stimuli. Every blue input has a 1 in bit 2 of at least one stimulus.
- **Y2 = bit 1.** In X6-Y2-Z3, every red input has 0 in bit 1 of both stimuli, and every blue input has at least one 1 there.
- **Y3 = bit 3.** In X6-Y3-Z2, the red inputs are exactly those with 0 in bit 3 of both stimuli.
- **Y1 = bit 4.** This is shown under X2 below.

**X6 is "at least one is 1" or "neither is 1"**
- Across all three X6 tasks, the pair (0,0) gets one colour, and (0,1), (1,0) and (1,1) all get the other.
- Only those two rules split the pairs that way. No other rule fits.

**X2 is "exactly one is 1" or "both are the same"**
- In X2-Y2-Z4 (bit 1), pairs that differ give yellow and pairs that match give red.
- In X2-Y1-Z4, the same pattern holds on bit 4, which fixes Y1 = bit 4.
- In X2-Y1-Z1 (bit 4), pairs that differ give green and pairs that match give yellow.
- Only those two rules split the pairs that way.

**Z3 depends on X6**
- If X6 is "at least one is 1", then Z3 gives blue when true and red when false.
- If X6 is "neither is 1", then Z3 gives red when true and blue when false.

**Checking the Z components**
- Z1, Z2, Z3 and Z4 come out different from each other under all four combinations.
- So the rule that different versions must differ does not rule out any combination.

**The new task, X2-Y4-Z3, reads bit 2. Four assignments survive:**

| X6 | X2 | Bit 2 differs → | Bit 2 matches → |
|---|---|---|---|
| at least one is 1 | exactly one is 1 | blue | red |
| neither is 1 | both are the same | blue | red |
| at least one is 1 | both are the same | red | blue |
| neither is 1 | exactly one is 1 | red | blue |

Two of the four give "differs → blue" and two give "differs → red", so the examples cannot decide. I chose "differs → blue" (matches → red) because it is the more natural reading. It has about a 50% chance of being right.

# Learn tasks from examples

Each task maps an input to one of four buttons: blue, red, green, or yellow. An input is a pair of stimuli; each stimulus has 4 binary features, written as 4 bits (bit positions 1-4, left to right). The line `1011 0110 -> green` means: stimulus 1 is 1011, stimulus 2 is 0110, and the correct button is green.

Every task is built from three components. A **Y component** picks one of the 4 features (bit positions 1-4); the task looks at that feature in both stimuli. An **X component** is a rule on those two bits, one of: both are 1; at least one is 1; exactly one is 1; neither is 1; not both are 1; both are the same. A **Z component** gives one button when the rule is true and a different button when it is false. A task's label lists its components, for example X2-Y1-Z3. Each kind has several versions (X1, X2, and so on); different versions of a kind are different from each other, and the same label always means the same component. You are not told which version does what.
